cards.q: Pregnancy: effect on gastrointestinal motility and oral absorption
cards.a: Motility reduced; oral absorption delayed

cards.q: Pregnancy: effect on plasma and extracellular fluid volume and drug distribution
cards.a: Fluid volume expands; volume of distribution may increase

cards.q: Pregnancy: plasma protein changes and effect on free drug
cards.a: Albumin falls and alpha-1 acid glycoprotein rises; free fraction of acidic drugs rises, basic drugs fall

cards.q: Pregnancy: renal blood flow effect on polar drugs
cards.a: Renal blood flow rises markedly; polar drugs eliminated faster

cards.q: Pregnancy: hepatic enzyme effect on drug metabolism
cards.a: Hepatic microsomal enzymes induced; many drugs metabolised faster

cards.q: Drug passage across placenta: main physicochemical factors
cards.a: Lipid solubility and degree of ionisation

cards.q: Thiopental at caesarean section: placental passage and neonatal effect
cards.a: Crosses almost immediately; sedation or apnoea in newborn

cards.q: Highly ionised drugs (succinylcholine, tubocurarine): placental passage
cards.a: Cross slowly; very low fetal concentrations

cards.q: Why salicylate, almost fully ionised, still crosses the placenta readily
cards.a: Its small unionised fraction is highly lipid-soluble

cards.q: Placental transfer by molecular weight: 250-500 Da
cards.a: Cross readily, depending on lipid solubility and ionisation

cards.q: Placental transfer by molecular weight: 500-1000 Da and above 1000 Da
cards.a: 500-1000 cross with more difficulty; above 1000 cross very poorly

cards.q: Anticoagulant of choice in pregnancy, and why
cards.a: Heparin: large polar molecule, does not cross placenta

cards.q: Placental transporters for immunoglobulins: when they develop
cards.a: From the second trimester, carrying large antibodies to the fetus

cards.q: Biological drugs (anti-TNF) crossing the placenta: risks reported
cards.a: Neonatal neutropenia, anaemia, thrombocytopenia; fetal BCG dissemination

cards.q: Ion trapping across placenta: maternal and fetal blood pH
cards.a: Maternal 7.4, fetal 7.3; basic drugs with pKa above 7.4 accumulate in fetus

cards.q: P-glycoprotein (MDR1) in placenta: effect on fetal drug levels
cards.a: Pumps drugs (vinblastine, doxorubicin) back into maternal blood, lowering fetal levels

cards.q: Protease inhibitors (HIV) and fetal levels: clinical concern
cards.a: Low fetal concentrations; may increase risk of vertical HIV transmission

cards.q: Glyburide: why fetal levels are lower than maternal
cards.a: Efflux by BCRP and MRP3 transporters, and very high maternal protein binding (over 98.8%)

cards.q: Drugs with higher protein binding in maternal than fetal plasma: list
cards.a: Sulfonamides, barbiturates, phenytoin, local anaesthetics

cards.q: Transfer of very lipid-soluble drugs depends on what
cards.a: Placental blood flow, not free drug concentration

cards.q: Placental metabolism: pentobarbital and toxic metabolites
cards.a: Placenta oxidises pentobarbital; can create toxic metabolites (e.g. ethanol, benzpyrenes)

cards.q: Prednisolone in pregnancy: why fetal exposure to active steroid is limited
cards.a: Placenta converts prednisolone to inactive prednisone

cards.q: Umbilical venous blood entering the fetal liver
cards.a: About 40-60%; the rest bypasses the liver

cards.q: Maternal drug effects in pregnancy: which tissues are altered
cards.a: Reproductive tissues (endocrine environment); other maternal organ effects not changed much

cards.q: Drugs needed in pregnancy for maternal heart failure or gestational diabetes
cards.a: Cardiac glycosides and diuretics; insulin

cards.q: Corticosteroid given to mother to stimulate fetal lung maturation
cards.a: When preterm birth is expected

cards.q: Phenobarbital given to mother near term: neonatal effect
cards.a: Induces fetal hepatic glucuronidation; less neonatal jaundice

cards.q: Maternal antiarrhythmics for fetal arrhythmia: examples
cards.a: Digoxin, flecainide, procainamide, verapamil (case series only)

cards.q: Maternal antiretroviral therapy: effect on HIV transmission to fetus
cards.a: Substantially reduces transmission; needs infant treatment too

cards.q: Chronic maternal opioid use: neonatal outcome
cards.a: Neonatal abstinence syndrome (neonatal dependence and withdrawal)

cards.q: ACE inhibitors in late pregnancy: fetal risk
cards.a: Significant irreversible fetal renal damage; contraindicated in second and third trimesters

cards.q: Diethylstilbestrol exposure in utero: delayed effect
cards.a: Adenocarcinoma (clear cell) of vagina in exposed female offspring after puberty

cards.q: Teratogenicity: definition
cards.a: Capacity of a drug to cause fetal abnormalities when given to the pregnant mother

cards.q: Placenta as a barrier to drugs
cards.a: Not a strict barrier; any drug crosses to some extent

cards.q: Fetal drug effects: stage 1 (fertilisation and implantation)
cards.a: Conception to 17 days; pregnancy failure, often unnoticed

cards.q: Fetal drug effects: organogenesis window
cards.a: 18 to 55 days; most vulnerable; deformities produced

cards.q: Fetal drug effects: growth and development stage onward
cards.a: From 56 days; developmental and functional abnormalities

cards.q: ACE inhibitors in growth stage: fetal effect
cards.a: Hypoplasia of organs, especially lungs and kidneys

cards.q: NSAIDs in late fetal life: fetal effect
cards.a: Premature closure of ductus arteriosus

cards.q: Androgens and progestins in fetal life: effect on female fetus
cards.a: Masculinisation (virilisation)

cards.q: Antithyroid drugs and lithium: fetal effect
cards.a: Fetal goitre

cards.q: Thalidomide: fetal period of limb development affected (Katzung)
cards.a: Weeks 4-7 of gestation, when arms and legs develop; phocomelia

cards.q: Thalidomide: defect caused
cards.a: Phocomelia (seal-like limbs)

cards.q: Tetracyclines in pregnancy: fetal effect
cards.a: Discoloured and deformed teeth; retarded bone growth

cards.q: Phenytoin in pregnancy: named fetal syndrome
cards.a: Fetal hydantoin syndrome

cards.q: Alcohol in pregnancy: fetal effect
cards.a: Fetal alcohol spectrum disorder; CNS, growth and facial development affected

cards.q: Vitamin A analogues (isotretinoin, etretinate): status as teratogens
cards.a: Powerful human teratogens

cards.q: Teratogen defined: three criteria
cards.a: Characteristic malformations (organ selectivity); stage-specific action in organogenesis; dose-dependent incidence

cards.q: Teratogenic effects beyond major malformations: examples
cards.a: Growth restriction (smoking), miscarriage (alcohol), stillbirth (smoke), neurocognitive delay (alcohol, valproic acid)

cards.q: Most drugs implicated as teratogens are
cards.a: Low-grade teratogens that only slightly raise malformation rates

cards.q: Foetal exposure to teratogen depends on
cards.a: Blood level and duration of drug in maternal circulation

cards.q: Background rate of congenital abnormality in all pregnancies (KDT8)
cards.a: About 2%

cards.q: Baseline teratogenic risk with no known exposure (Katzung)
cards.a: About 3% risk of neonatal abnormality

cards.q: Human teratogenic drugs listed in KDT8: list
cards.a: Thalidomide, anticancer drugs (methotrexate), androgens, progestins, stilboestrol, tetracyclines, warfarin, phenytoin, phenobarbitone, carbamazepine, valproate, alcohol, ACE inhibitors, lithium, antithyroid drugs, indomethacin/aspirin, isotretinoin

cards.q: Drugs with significant teratogenic or other fetal adverse effects (Katzung table): list
cards.a: ACE inhibitors, aminopterin, amphetamines, androgens, tricyclic antidepressants, barbiturates, busulfan, carbamazepine, chlorpropamide, clomipramine, cocaine, cyclophosphamide, cytarabine, diazepam, dydrogesterone, diethylstilbestrol, ethanol, etretinate, heroin, iodide, isotretinoin, lithium, methadone, methotrexate, misoprostol, mycophenolate mofetil, organic solvents, penicillamine, phencyclidine, phenytoin, propylthiouracil, SSRIs, smoking, tamoxifen, tetracycline, thalidomide, trimethadione, topiramate, valproic acid, warfarin

cards.q: Folic acid before and during early pregnancy: effect on neural tube defects
cards.a: Reduces neural tube defects by up to 75%

cards.q: Non-drug teratogens: infections
cards.a: Rubella, cytomegalovirus, herpes, Zika virus

cards.q: Non-drug teratogens: chemicals and physical factors
cards.a: Heavy metals (mercury, lead), radiation, hyperthermia

cards.q: Untreated maternal condition as a teratogenic cause
cards.a: Untreated hypertension of pregnancy raises major malformation rates

cards.q: FDA pregnancy categories (old system): range
cards.a: A (safe) to X (contraindicated); five categories

cards.q: FDA category A: meaning
cards.a: Controlled studies in women show no first-trimester risk; fetal harm appears remote

cards.q: FDA category D: meaning
cards.a: Positive evidence of human fetal risk; use may be acceptable in life-threatening or serious disease

cards.q: FDA category X: meaning
cards.a: Risk clearly outweighs benefit; contraindicated in women who are or may become pregnant

cards.q: FDA pregnancy labelling change: effective date and what it removed
cards.a: 30 June 2015; letter categories (A, B, C, D, X) removed

cards.q: New FDA pregnancy label sections
cards.a: Risk Summary, Clinical Considerations and Data; includes pregnancy-registry data

cards.q: Counselling: how many drugs are proven human teratogens
cards.a: Fewer than 30; hundreds proven safe

cards.q: Counselling risk: stopping SSRI therapy for depression in pregnancy
cards.a: Led to serious maternal morbidity

cards.q: Teratogen advice principle in pregnancy (KDT8)
cards.a: Avoid all drugs unless compelling reason, regardless of category

cards.q: Mutagenic and carcinogenic drugs: approval status
cards.a: Generally not approved or withdrawn, unless used in life-threatening conditions

cards.q: Mutagenicity and carcinogenicity: mechanism
cards.a: Reactive intermediates from oxidation covalently modify DNA

cards.q: Chemical carcinogenesis: time to develop
cards.a: Usually 10-40 years

cards.q: Drugs implicated in mutagenicity or carcinogenicity (KDT8): list
cards.a: Anticancer drugs, radioisotopes, oestrogens, tobacco

cards.q: Drugs in breast milk: usual neonatal effect
cards.a: Most are in amounts too small to harm; formula feeding carries higher morbidity and mortality

cards.q: Rule of thumb: infant dose from milk considered negligible
cards.a: Under 10% of maternal weight-corrected dose

cards.q: Timing of a safe drug in breastfeeding mothers
cards.a: Take 30-60 min after nursing; 3-4 h before next feed

cards.q: Drugs with clinically meaningful exposure in breast milk: list
cards.a: Lithium, amiodarone, atenolol

cards.q: Tetracycline during breastfeeding: infant risk
cards.a: Permanent staining of developing teeth; avoid

cards.q: Isoniazid in breast milk: infant effect and prevention
cards.a: Pyridoxine deficiency in infant; give pyridoxine to mother

cards.q: Hypnotic doses of barbiturates in breast milk: infant effect
cards.a: Lethargy, sedation and poor suck reflex

cards.q: Diazepam in breastfeeding: infant risk
cards.a: Sedation; long half-life causes accumulation

cards.q: Chloral hydrate and breastfeeding timing
cards.a: Sedation if infant fed at peak milk concentration

cards.q: Methadone in breastfeeding: approach
cards.a: Can be given under supervision; do not stop abruptly; monitor infant for withdrawal

cards.q: Opioids (heroin, methadone, morphine) in breast milk: risk
cards.a: Can prolong neonatal opioid dependence after chronic maternal use

cards.q: Codeine in breastfeeding: why neonatal death occurred
cards.a: Mother was an ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metaboliser, making much more morphine

cards.q: Why neonates are more sensitive to morphine in brain
cards.a: Low P-glycoprotein at the neonatal blood-brain barrier, so more morphine enters the brain

cards.q: Lithium in breast milk: concentration relative to serum
cards.a: Equal to maternal serum; infant exposure can be large

cards.q: Radioactive iodine and breastfeeding
cards.a: Thyroid suppression in infant; breastfeeding contraindicated after large doses; withheld days to weeks after small doses

cards.q: Radioiodine exposure via milk: later thyroid cancer risk
cards.a: Can increase risk of later thyroid cancer as much as 10-fold

cards.q: Breastfeeding during cancer chemotherapy or immunomodulating drugs
cards.a: Avoid breastfeeding

cards.q: Chloramphenicol in breastfeeding: advice
cards.a: Recommended not to take while breastfeeding (marrow suppression risk)

cards.q: Maternal alcohol and nicotine during breastfeeding
cards.a: Minimal alcohol not reported to harm; excess sedates infant; nicotine concentrations low

cards.q: Caffeine in breast milk
cards.a: Very small amounts; moderate intake considered safe

cards.q: Neonatal glomerular filtration (per surface area) compared with adult
cards.a: 30-40% of adult value; lower still before 34 weeks gestation

cards.q: Glomerular filtration reaches adult value (Katzung)
cards.a: By 6-12 months of age (per unit surface area)

cards.q: Filtration and tubular secretion maturity (KDT8)
cards.a: Glomerular filtration adult by about 5 months; tubular secretion about 7 months

cards.q: Renally excreted drugs in newborn: half-life effect (KDT8)
cards.a: Gentamicin and penicillin half-lives prolonged 3-5 times

cards.q: Penicillin clearance in preterm infants
cards.a: 17% of adult rate by surface area; 34% when adjusted for body weight

cards.q: Ampicillin dose for neonate under 7 days
cards.a: 50-100 mg/kg/day in two doses at 12-hour intervals

cards.q: Ampicillin dose for neonate over 7 days
cards.a: 100-200 mg/kg/day in three doses at 8-hour intervals

cards.q: Gentamicin dose for neonate under 7 days
cards.a: 5 mg/kg/day in two doses at 12-hour intervals

cards.q: Gentamicin dose for neonate over 7 days
cards.a: 7.5 mg/kg/day in three doses at 8-hour intervals

cards.q: Digoxin in children vs adults: daily dose per kg
cards.a: Children 8-12 micrograms/kg; adults 3-5 micrograms/kg

cards.q: Digoxin in neonates and infants: why it accumulates
cards.a: Clearance depends on renal function; accumulation if glomerular filtration falls

cards.q: Intramuscular absorption in sick preterm infants
cards.a: Irregular and unpredictable; sudden perfusion gain can cause toxic levels

cards.q: Drugs especially hazardous with unpredictable IM absorption in sick infants: list
cards.a: Cardiac glycosides, aminoglycosides, anticonvulsants

cards.q: Neonatal gastric emptying time in first days
cards.a: Prolonged, up to 6-8 hours

cards.q: Gastric acid secretion in preterm infants: peak
cards.a: Slower to start; highest concentrations on day 4

cards.q: Neonatal oral absorption compared with older children: decreased drugs
cards.a: Acetaminophen, phenobarbital, phenytoin

cards.q: Neonatal oral absorption compared with older children: increased drugs
cards.a: Ampicillin and penicillin G; normal for diazepam, digoxin, sulfonamides

cards.q: Infant skin and rectal route absorption
cards.a: Transdermal absorption faster (thin skin); rectal absorption fast and predictable

cards.q: Rectal diazepam in children: use
cards.a: Controls febrile seizures in children under 5 years

cards.q: Neonatal body water and extracellular fluid (% of body weight)
cards.a: Total water 70-75% (adult 50-60%); extracellular 40% (adult 20%)

cards.q: Fat content of preterm vs full-term infant
cards.a: About 1% vs 15% of body weight; lipophilic drugs accumulate less

cards.q: Neonatal protein binding and free drug
cards.a: Protein binding reduced (e.g. diazepam, phenytoin, ampicillin); free fraction rises

cards.q: Worked example: free drug at 300 mcg/L total, 98% vs 90% bound
cards.a: Free drug 6 vs 30 mcg/L, five times higher in the infant

cards.q: Sulfonamides given to preterm neonates: serious adverse effect
cards.a: Displaced bilirubin entering brain: kernicterus

cards.q: Ceftriaxone in neonates: age restriction
cards.a: Avoided completely under 2 months of age

cards.q: Rising bilirubin and phenytoin: effect
cards.a: Bilirubin displaces phenytoin; free drug concentration rises

cards.q: Neonatal liver drug metabolism: relative capacity
cards.a: 50-70% of adult values in early neonatal life

cards.q: Glucuronide formation reaches adult values (per kg) by
cards.a: Third to fourth year of life

cards.q: Maternal enzyme-inducing drug (phenobarbital) and neonatal metabolism
cards.a: Neonate metabolises faster; less effect at usual neonatal dose

cards.q: Toddler drug metabolism (12-36 months) vs adults
cards.a: Often exceeds adult values, needing larger mg/kg doses

cards.q: Children: half-lives of which drugs are shorter than in adults (KDT8)
cards.a: Theophylline, phenytoin, carbamazepine

cards.q: Neonatal opioid sensitivity: relation to age
cards.a: More sensitive than older children and adults to central depressant effects

cards.q: Indomethacin in neonates: effect on ductus arteriosus
cards.a: Rapidly closes patent ductus arteriosus

cards.q: Prostaglandin E1 infusion in neonates: purpose and adverse effect
cards.a: Keeps ductus open in transposition or tetralogy; antral hyperplasia with gastric outlet obstruction (dose-dependent)

cards.q: Elixir vs suspension: uniformity of dose
cards.a: Elixirs are solutions and need no shaking; suspensions must be shaken before each dose

cards.q: Phenytoin suspension: risk from uneven distribution
cards.a: Early doses too weak, late doses toxic

cards.q: Household teaspoons: measured volume range
cards.a: 2.5 to 7.8 mL; use a calibrated spoon or syringe

cards.q: Antibiotic non-adherence in children: typical cause
cards.a: Child feels better after 4-5 days; course is 10-14 days, so parents stop early

cards.q: Paediatric dosing error: typical magnitude
cards.a: Typically 10-fold, from decimal-point mistakes

cards.q: Digoxin volume error: example of fatal risk
cards.a: 0.1 mL (5 micrograms) given as 1.0 mL

cards.q: Drugs needing independent double-checking of paediatric dose
cards.a: Narrow therapeutic window: digoxin, insulin, potassium

cards.q: Decimal-point rule in prescribing
cards.a: Leading zero before decimal (0.5); no trailing zero (5.0 written as 5)

cards.q: Paediatric dose upper limit
cards.a: Should never exceed the adult dose

cards.q: Best source of paediatric dose information
cards.a: Manufacturer's package insert; FDA Pediatric Rule (1998) pushed paediatric testing

cards.q: Young's rule for child dose
cards.a: Age / (age + 12) x adult dose

cards.q: Clark's rule for child dose
cards.a: Weight (lb) / 150 x adult dose

cards.q: Child dose by body weight (KDT8): preferred method and age formulae
cards.a: Dose by weight (mg/kg); age-based formulae no longer used

cards.q: Age, weight and surface-area dose estimates: reliability
cards.a: Age and weight rules tend to underestimate; surface area more likely adequate

cards.q: Children: adverse effects particular to growing children (KDT8)
cards.a: Growth suppression (corticosteroids); early epiphyseal fusion (androgens); tooth discolouration (tetracyclines); dystonic reactions (phenothiazines)

cards.q: Elderly: glomerular filtration (KDT8)
cards.a: About 75% of young-adult value at 50 years; about 50% at 75

cards.q: Streptomycin daily dose in elderly
cards.a: 0.75 g after 50 years, 0.5 g after 70 years (vs 1 g young adults)

cards.q: Elderly: hepatic changes and first-pass drugs
cards.a: Reduced microsomal activity and liver blood flow; oral bioavailability of high-extraction drugs rises

cards.q: Elderly: why cumulative toxicity occurs
cards.a: Lower renal and metabolic clearance during prolonged medication

cards.q: Elderly: absorption change
cards.a: Slower absorption (gut motility and intestinal blood flow reduced)

cards.q: Elderly: volume of distribution for lipophilic and hydrophilic drugs
cards.a: Lipophilic: increased; hydrophilic: decreased

cards.q: Elderly: plasma albumin and drug binding
cards.a: Albumin lower, so protein binding of weak acids falls; alpha-1 acid glycoprotein may rise for basic drugs

cards.q: Elderly: digitalis sensitivity
cards.a: Relatively intolerant to digitalis

cards.q: Elderly: responsiveness to beta-adrenoceptor drugs
cards.a: Reduced response to both beta-agonists and antagonists

cards.q: Elderly males with prostatism: anticholinergic risk
cards.a: Even mild anticholinergic activity worsens voiding difficulty

cards.q: Elderly: common adverse CNS effects
cards.a: Postural instability, giddiness and mental confusion

cards.q: Elderly: homeostasis change with exercise
cards.a: Cardiac output rises mainly by stroke volume, not tachycardia

cards.q: Orthostatic hypotension: definition and check
cards.a: Fall of more than 20 mm Hg systolic on standing; check at every visit

cards.q: Elderly: tolerance of hypothermia
cards.a: Poorly tolerated

cards.q: Renal function vs serum creatinine in the elderly
cards.a: Serum creatinine alone is inadequate; falling muscle mass lowers creatinine production

cards.q: Cockcroft-Gault estimate: formula
cards.a: (140 - age) x weight (kg) / (72 x serum creatinine mg/dL); x0.85 for women

cards.q: Cockcroft-Gault estimate: age range and limitation
cards.a: Applies age 40-80; only a population estimate, about one-third of elderly have normal renal function

cards.q: Correcting an elderly dose for reduced renal clearance (Katzung)
cards.a: Young-adult dose x eGFR/100

cards.q: Dehydration and renal drug clearance in the elderly
cards.a: Can reduce clearance markedly; reversible with rehydration

cards.q: Elderly anaesthesia: why IV agents are preferred over inhalation
cards.a: Reduced respiratory capacity and active pulmonary disease

cards.q: Benzodiazepine and barbiturate half-lives with age
cards.a: Increase by 50-150% between ages 30 and 70, mostly from 60 to 70

cards.q: Hepatic clearance reduced with age (Katzung table): list
cards.a: Alprazolam, barbiturates, carbenoxolone, chlordiazepoxide, chlormethiazole, clobazam, desmethyldiazepam, diazepam, flurazepam, imipramine, meperidine, nortriptyline, phenylbutazone, propranolol, quinidine, quinine, theophylline, tolbutamide

cards.q: Hepatic clearance NOT changed with age (Katzung table): list
cards.a: Ethanol, isoniazid, lidocaine, lorazepam, nitrazepam, oxazepam, prazosin, salicylate, warfarin

cards.q: Lorazepam and oxazepam in the elderly
cards.a: Less affected by age-related changes than other benzodiazepines

cards.q: Elderly and opioids: main concern
cards.a: Respiratory depression, so start cautiously and titrate

cards.q: Chlorpromazine in the elderly: orthostatic hypotension and dosing
cards.a: Alpha-blockade causes orthostatic hypotension; start at a fraction of the young-adult dose

cards.q: Haloperidol in elderly with preexisting extrapyramidal disease
cards.a: Increased extrapyramidal toxicity; avoid

cards.q: Lithium in elderly: dose adjustment and thiazide interaction
cards.a: Renally cleared; thiazides reduce lithium clearance, so cut dose and check levels more often

cards.q: Antidepressant choice in elderly
cards.a: SSRIs preferred by some (fewer autonomic effects); if TCA, use nortriptyline or desipramine

cards.q: Essential tremor in elderly: drugs that help
cards.a: Beta-blockers (propranolol) and some benzodiazepines (alprazolam)

cards.q: Antihypertensive first step in elderly
cards.a: Thiazide at low dose; watch hypokalaemia, hyperglycaemia, hyperuricaemia

cards.q: Antihypertensives in elderly: calcium channel blockers
cards.a: Effective and safe when titrated; useful with atherosclerotic angina

cards.q: Beta-blockers in elderly: concern
cards.a: Hazardous in obstructive airway disease; less useful than CCBs unless chronic heart failure

cards.q: ACE inhibitors in elderly: when useful
cards.a: Less useful unless heart failure or diabetes is present

cards.q: Digoxin in elderly: changes in kinetics
cards.a: Clearance usually lower; half-life up 50% or more; loading dose reduced

cards.q: Digoxin in elderly: pharmacodynamic change
cards.a: No increase in therapeutic sensitivity; increased risk of arrhythmia

cards.q: Antiarrhythmics in elderly: disopyramide
cards.a: Avoid: antimuscarinic (voiding problems in men) and negative inotropy

cards.q: Lidocaine in elderly: loading dose
cards.a: Half-life increased; reduce loading dose

cards.q: Aminoglycoside half-life in elderly
cards.a: Gentamicin, kanamycin and netilmicin more than doubled; tobramycin less so

cards.q: NSAIDs in elderly: toxicities
cards.a: Aspirin: GI irritation and bleeding; newer NSAIDs: renal damage that may be irreversible

cards.q: COX-2 selective NSAIDs and renal safety in elderly
cards.a: No evidence they are safer for the kidney

cards.q: Corticosteroids in elderly: dose-related toxicity
cards.a: Osteoporosis, dose- and duration-related

cards.q: Antibiotics in elderly: pharmacokinetic change
cards.a: Beta-lactams, aminoglycosides and fluoroquinolones cleared by kidney, so half-lives rise

cards.q: Vaccines for older adults (Katzung)
cards.a: Influenza yearly; tetanus every 10 years; pneumococcal and zoster once

cards.q: Adverse drug reactions with number of drugs taken (elderly)
cards.a: Rise from about 10% with one drug to nearly 100% with ten

cards.q: ADR incidence in elderly compared with younger people
cards.a: At least twice as high

cards.q: Brown bag analysis: what it is and typical result
cards.a: Patient brings all medicines; total can often be cut by 30-50%

cards.q: Cimetidine in elderly: two problems
cards.a: More confusion and slurred speech; inhibits hepatic metabolism (phenytoin, warfarin, beta-blockers)

cards.q: Herbal ginkgo and aspirin in elderly
cards.a: Increased bleeding risk

cards.q: Geriatric prescribing principle 1
cards.a: Take a careful drug history (drug-induced disease, interactions)

cards.q: Geriatric prescribing principle 3: titration and waiting
cards.a: Start small, titrate; wait at least three age-adjusted half-lives before increasing dose

cards.q: Geriatric prescribing principle: if no response at normal dose
cards.a: Check blood level; if no response at therapeutic level, switch drug

cards.q: Geriatric prescribing principle: simplify regimen
cards.a: Use drugs taken at the same time of day; reduce number of drugs

cards.q: Elderly and dosing aids
cards.a: Use a dosing syringe if tremor or motor disability; large labels for poor vision

cards.q: Liver disease: effect on bioavailability of high first-pass drugs
cards.a: Increased, from loss of hepatocellular function and portocaval shunting

cards.q: Liver disease: protein binding of acidic drugs
cards.a: Reduced (lower albumin); more free drug (e.g. diclofenac, warfarin)

cards.q: Liver disease: drugs whose metabolism and elimination fall, so dose should be reduced: list
cards.a: Morphine, lidocaine, propranolol

cards.q: Liver disease: preferred alternatives
cards.a: Oxazepam or lorazepam instead of diazepam; atenolol instead of propranolol

cards.q: Prodrugs needing hepatic activation in liver disease
cards.a: Less effective; avoid (e.g. bacampicillin)

cards.q: Liver disease: test to estimate drug handling
cards.a: None simple, unlike creatinine clearance for kidney disease

cards.q: Cirrhosis: CNS sensitivity to morphine and barbiturates
cards.a: Markedly increased; normal doses can cause coma

cards.q: Brisk diuresis in impending hepatic encephalopathy: mechanism
cards.a: Hypokalaemic alkalosis converts NH4+ to NH3, which enters brain

cards.q: Oral anticoagulants in liver disease
cards.a: Markedly prolong prothrombin time; clotting factors already low

cards.q: Liver disease: drugs whose fluid-retaining or acidosis effects worsen
cards.a: Phenylbutazone (and other NSAIDs) fluid retention; metformin lactic acidosis

cards.q: Liver disease: general drug advice
cards.a: Avoid hepatotoxic drugs

cards.q: Renal disease: clearance of drugs excreted unchanged
cards.a: Falls in parallel with creatinine clearance (e.g. aminoglycosides, digoxin, phenobarbitone)

cards.q: Renal failure: loading and maintenance dose rule
cards.a: Loading dose unchanged (unless oedema); reduce maintenance dose or extend interval

cards.q: Renal guideline: dose rate as % of normal by creatinine clearance (ml/min)
Renal failure: drugs only partly excreted unchanged
cards.a: Dose rate reduced, but to a lesser extent

cards.q: Renal failure: effect on steady-state with long half-life
cards.a: Steady state reached more slowly with maintenance doses

cards.q: Renal disease: protein binding change
cards.a: Acidic drug binding reduced; basic drug binding little changed

cards.q: Renal failure: blood-brain barrier and CNS depressants
cards.a: More permeable; opiates, barbiturates, phenothiazines, benzodiazepines cause more CNS depression

cards.q: Pethidine in renal failure: why avoid
cards.a: Norpethidine accumulates on repeated dosing, causing seizures and twitching

cards.q: Renal failure: postural hypotension
cards.a: Antihypertensives cause greater postural hypotension

cards.q: Drugs that worsen uraemia or fluid retention in renal failure
cards.a: Tetracyclines (anti-anabolic, worsen uraemia); NSAIDs (fluid retention)

cards.q: Antimicrobials needing dose reduction even in mild renal failure: list
cards.a: Aminoglycosides, cephalexin, ethambutol, vancomycin, amphotericin B, acyclovir

cards.q: Antimicrobials needing dose reduction only in severe renal failure: list
cards.a: Cotrimoxazole, carbenicillin, cefotaxime, norfloxacin, ciprofloxacin, metronidazole

cards.q: Potentially nephrotoxic drugs to avoid in kidney disease: list
cards.a: Aminoglycosides, tetracyclines (except doxycycline), sulfonamides, vancomycin, nitrofurantoin, cyclosporine, amphotericin B

cards.q: Sulfonamides in kidney disease: concern
cards.a: Crystalluria

cards.q: Thiazides in renal failure: advice
cards.a: Ineffective and can worsen uraemia; use furosemide

cards.q: Potassium-sparing diuretics in renal failure
cards.a: Contraindicated: hyperkalaemia and cardiac depression

cards.q: Urinary antiseptics that give systemic toxicity in renal failure: list
cards.a: Nalidixic acid, nitrofurantoin, methenamine mandelate (fail to reach high urine levels)

cards.q: Heart failure: effect on drug absorption
cards.a: Reduced by mucosal oedema and splanchnic vasoconstriction (procainamide, hydrochlorothiazide)

cards.q: Heart failure: loading doses of lidocaine and procainamide
cards.a: Should be lowered (volume of distribution changes)

cards.q: Heart failure: drugs whose elimination is retarded (dose reduction)
cards.a: Lidocaine, procainamide, theophylline

cards.q: Decompensated heart: digitalis sensitivity
cards.a: More sensitive to digitalis

cards.q: Hypothyroidism: drug sensitivity
cards.a: More sensitive to digoxin, morphine and CNS depressants

cards.q: Hyperthyroidism: digoxin response
cards.a: Resistant to digoxin's inotropic action but more prone to its arrhythmias

cards.q: Hyperthyroidism: catecholamine and digitalis response
cards.a: More prone to adrenaline- and digitalis-induced arrhythmias

cards.q: Digoxin clearance and thyroid function
cards.a: Roughly proportional to thyroid function; only partly explains sensitivity changes

cards.q: Coeliac disease and drug absorption
cards.a: Amoxicillin absorption falls; cephalexin and cotrimoxazole absorption rises

cards.q: Migraine attack: effect on drug absorption
cards.a: Gastric stasis delays absorption

cards.q: Achlorhydria and aspirin absorption
cards.a: Decreases absorption by favouring its ionisation

cards.q: NSAIDs in peptic ulcer disease
cards.a: Can aggravate ulcer disease

cards.q: Myasthenia gravis: sensitivity to neuromuscular blockers
cards.a: Very sensitive to curare-type drugs

cards.q: Drugs taken in pregnancy for maternal physiological change: principle (Katzung)
cards.a: Drug effects on non-reproductive maternal organs usually unchanged, but physiology changes the need

cards.q: Child-Pugh score parameters: list all
cards.a: Bilirubin, albumin, INR, ascites, encephalopathy

cards.q: Child-Pugh class A (mild): points
cards.a: 5-6 points

cards.q: Child-Pugh class B (moderate): points
cards.a: 7-9 points

cards.q: Child-Pugh class C (severe): points
cards.a: 10-15 points

cards.q: Child-Pugh classes B and C indicate
cards.a: Decompensated cirrhosis

cards.q: Ponesimod: not recommended in which hepatic impairment
cards.a: Moderate or severe (Child-Pugh B or C)

cards.q: Obeticholic acid: when used
cards.a: No adequate response to ursodeoxycholic acid after at least 1 year, or UDCA intolerance

cards.q: Obeticholic acid start: non-cirrhotic or Child-Pugh A
cards.a: 5 mg once daily for 3 months; then up to 10 mg once daily

cards.q: Obeticholic acid start: Child-Pugh B or C, or prior decompensation
cards.a: 5 mg once weekly for 3 months; then 5 mg twice weekly, max 10 mg twice weekly, doses 3+ days apart

cards.q: Succinylcholine in hepatic failure: why unsafe
cards.a: Liver-made plasma pseudocholinesterase, which breaks it down, is deficient

cards.q: Succinylcholine: other organ failure where unsafe
cards.a: Renal failure

cards.q: Antitubercular drugs safe in liver disease
cards.a: Streptomycin and ethambutol

cards.q: Antitubercular drugs by hepatotoxicity, most to least: list all
cards.a: Pyrazinamide, isoniazid, rifampicin

cards.q: TB with liver damage: starting regimen: list all
cards.a: Streptomycin, levofloxacin, ethambutol

cards.q: TB with liver damage: reintroduction order as transaminases normalise: list all
cards.a: Rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide

cards.q: Fluoroquinolones removed in bile and contraindicated in liver disease: list all
cards.a: Pefloxacin, moxifloxacin, trovafloxacin

cards.q: Trovafloxacin status
cards.a: Banned because of hepatotoxicity

cards.q: Dose for exceptionally obese or lean adult: formula
cards.a: Individual dose = (body weight kg / 70) x average adult dose

cards.q: Body-size dosing basis argued to be more accurate than body weight
cards.a: Body surface area

cards.q: Vancomycin with non-high-flux haemodialysis: typical schedule
cards.a: About 1 g (around 15 mg/kg) every 5 to 7 days

cards.q: Vancomycin with intermittent high-efficiency or high-flux dialysis
cards.a: Maintenance dose needed after each dialysis session

cards.q: Dosage forms difficult for young children: list all
cards.a: Solid dosage forms; metered-dose inhalers
